lead: A head-up display (HUD) projects flight symbols onto a glass combiner in front of the pilot, so the pilot reads speed, attitude and guidance while looking at the runway or the target. The symbols are collimated: they appear at infinity, at the same focus as the outside world. A helmet-mounted display (HMD) puts the symbols on the helmet visor or an eyepiece, and a head tracker keeps them pointing at the right place wherever the pilot looks. Civil aircraft use HUDs mainly for low-visibility approach and landing; military aircraft use HUDs and HMDs for weapon aiming, cueing and night flying.
prereq: You need: Electronic displays: PFD, MFD, EADI and EHSI for the symbols the HUD repeats.

sections.h3: How a HUD puts symbols at infinity

blocks.text: A HUD has four parts. The HUD computer (symbol generator) builds the picture from air data, inertial and guidance data. The display source (a CRT in older units, now an LCD with LED backlight or a micromirror projector) draws the symbols brightly. The collimating optics are lenses or curved mirrors with the source at their focal plane, so the rays from each symbol point leave parallel. The combiner is a glass plate with a coating that reflects the display colour (usually green) and transmits the rest of the outside light.

Parallel rays look as if they come from a very distant object, so the symbols form a virtual image at infinity. The pilot's eye can stay focused on the runway and still see sharp symbols. A panel display 0.75 m away needs a focus change of 1 ÷ 0.75 = 1.33 dioptres every time the eyes move between it and the outside, and the eyes also have to move down. The HUD removes both.

Fighters use a refractive HUD: the optics sit under the glareshield and the combiner stands above them. Airliners use an overhead (reflective) HUD: a projector above the pilot's head and a combiner that folds down in front of the eyes. The eye box (head motion box) is the space in which the pilot's eyes can move and still see all the symbols; the exit aperture of the optics limits the instantaneous field of view.

blocks.where: IFOV is the instantaneous field of view in degrees; D is the diameter of the exit aperture (collimating lens) in mm; L is the distance from the eye to that aperture in mm.

sections.h3: Conformal symbols and the flight path vector

blocks.text: Conformal symbols are drawn where the real thing is in the outside world: the horizon line, the pitch ladder, the runway outline and the flight path vector (FPV), which marks where the aircraft is actually going. Non-conformal symbols sit at fixed places: airspeed, altitude, heading and mode labels. Conformal symbols are only useful if they are exactly aligned (boresighted) with the aircraft axes; a misaligned FPV points the pilot at the wrong spot on the runway.

blocks.where: γ is the flight path angle below the horizon; V<sub>v</sub> is the vertical speed and V<sub>g</sub> the ground speed, both in the same units (ft/min here, with 1 kt = 101.27 ft/min).

blocks.text: On a stable approach the pilot places the FPV on the touchdown zone. A HUD with guidance lets a suitably certified airliner land in fog with the pilot flying by hand, and an enhanced vision system can add an infrared image of the runway behind the symbols.

An HMD puts a small display and optics on the helmet: one eye (monocular, like the helicopter sight of the AH-64 Apache) or both eyes (binocular). A head tracker measures where the head points, by magnetic, optical or inertial sensing or a mix. The computer uses that direction to draw conformal symbols and to cue sensors and missiles off-boresight: the pilot looks at a target, presses a switch, and the seeker or radar slews to that line of sight. Night-vision HMDs add an image intensifier or a thermal image. The F-35 has no HUD at all; its HMD carries every head-up symbol.

The hard parts are mass (a heavy helmet strains the neck under g and in an ejection), fit, and tracker latency. If the computer draws a symbol for where the head was a few milliseconds ago, the symbol trails the real target whenever the head turns. The error is the head rate times the delay, so fast trackers and head-motion prediction are needed.

examples.question: An airliner flies an approach at a ground speed of 140 kt with a vertical speed of 750 ft/min down. Its overhead HUD has an exit aperture of D = 150 mm, and the pilot's eye is L = 600 mm from it. (a) Find the flight path angle γ, where the FPV sits below the horizon line. (b) Find the instantaneous field of view. (c) Is the FPV inside the instantaneous field of view when the pilot looks along the horizon?
steps: Ground speed in ft/min: 140 kt × 101.27 = 14 178 ft/min.
Flight path angle: γ = arctan(750 ÷ 14 178) = arctan(0.0529) = 3.03°. The FPV is drawn 3.03° below the horizon line, on the usual 3° glide path.
Half of the IFOV is 7.13° above and below the line of sight.
3.03° is less than 7.13°, so the FPV is inside the instantaneous field of view.
examples.answer: γ = 3.03° below the horizon; IFOV = 14.25° (±7.13°); the FPV is inside it with about 4° to spare.

examples.question: A fighter pilot turns the head at 100° per second. The HMD head tracker and graphics have a total latency of 30 ms. (a) Find the angular error of a conformal symbol while the head turns. (b) What total latency keeps the error at or below 0.5°?
examples.answer: The symbol trails by 3.0°; the latency must fall to 5 ms, or the computer must predict head motion, to keep the error within 0.5°.

traps: Writing that HUD symbols are focused on the combiner glass. They are collimated to infinity; the combiner only reflects them.
Saying the eye never refocuses with a HUD. It does not refocus between the symbols and the outside world; looking down at the panel still needs a focus change.
Using vertical speed in ft/min with ground speed in knots in arctan(V<sub>v</sub> ÷ V<sub>g</sub>). Convert first: 1 kt = 101.27 ft/min.
Calling the head tracker the display. It only measures head direction; its latency makes symbols swim.
Saying a HUD and an HMD are always fitted together. On the F-35 the HMD replaces the HUD.

quiz.q: Name the four parts of a HUD.
quiz.a: HUD computer (symbol generator), display source, collimating optics and combiner.

quiz.q: What is the eye box of a HUD?
quiz.a: The space in which the pilot's eyes can move and still see all the symbols.
So they appear at infinity, at the same focus as the outside scene, and the pilot can read them without refocusing between symbols and runway.

quiz.q: Give two conformal and two non-conformal HUD symbols.
quiz.a: Conformal: horizon line, flight path vector (also pitch ladder, runway outline). Non-conformal: airspeed, altitude (also heading, mode labels).

quiz.q: Ground speed 120 kt, vertical speed 640 ft/min down. Find the flight path angle.
A HUD aperture of 120 mm is 500 mm from the eye. Find the IFOV.
Why is boresight alignment critical for a HUD but not for a head-down PFD?
quiz.a: Conformal symbols claim to sit on real objects; a misaligned FPV or runway outline points the pilot at the wrong place. A PFD picture is not overlaid on the outside world, so a small offset does not mislead in the same way.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer HUDs use waveguide combiners that are much thinner and lighter than classic optics, and combined vision systems merge infrared and database terrain images. Helmet displays move towards wide binocular fields with fused thermal imagery and eye tracking. Search for 'waveguide HUD', 'enhanced flight vision system' and 'head tracker latency'.

figure.caption: A HUD seen from the side, drawn to the worked example's angles: the display source sits at the focal plane of the collimating lens, so the rays reaching the eye are parallel and the symbols appear at infinity. The flight path vector sits 3.03° below the horizon on the touchdown zone, inside the 14.25° instantaneous field of view.

spec.aria: Side view. At the bottom, a HUD computer feeds a display source under a collimating lens. Three parallel rays rise to a tilted combiner and reflect horizontally to the pilot's eye on the left. From the eye, a dashed horizon runs right, two dotted lines mark the instantaneous field of view of plus and minus 7.13 degrees, and a green line falls 3.03 degrees to the flight path vector symbol on the touchdown zone of a runway.
